taxonomy.note: Current Kew/POWO accepts Dalea purpurea and two infraspecific taxa, D. purpurea var. arenicola and D. purpurea var. purpurea. Keep this source concept at species rank unless an exact specimen/source supports a variety assignment.

target_zone_range.evidence_basis: BONAP/NAPA county mapping confirms a spotty native Texas distribution. Bell — Bell County East–Big Hill environmental assessment/USDA plant-community treatment lists Dalea purpurea in the Bell County project region. Concho and Tom Green — USDA NRCS Rolling Limestone Prairie ecological-site descriptions list Dalea purpurea in the native/reference plant community and explicitly ground those site descriptions in the Concho County (1988) and Tom Green County (1976) soil surveys.
target_zone_range.guardrail: PASS is for the project-wide target zone only. Current B122 evidence does not lock Hays, Travis, or Williamson County; do not label this taxon Hays-local from these sources. Concho/Tom Green support is ecological-site documentation rather than a newly inspected herbarium voucher, so preserve that evidence type in downstream notes.

morphology.look_here_first: Start at the flower head, then move straight to the calyx. Purple prairie clover forms dense thimble-like to cylindrical heads whose fresh flowers progress upward from the lower part of the head; the leaves are odd-pinnate with usually about 3–7 very narrow leaflets. For the difficult D. purpurea versus D. compacta split, use calyx pubescence rather than flower color.
best_field_traits: perennial/subshrub with stiff upright stems from a deep stout taproot
alternate odd-pinnate leaves with 3–7 very narrow leaflets
dense thimble-shaped to cylindrical terminal flower heads
flowers open from the bottom of the head upward, leaving older papery portions below
fruit is a small legume with one or two seeds
dry prairie, plains, hillsides and open woodland-edge settings within its Texas range
morphology.key_separation: D. compacta is the priority confuser: published Texas treatment notes that D. compacta has calyx hairs arranged in longitudinal lines separated by bald areas, whereas D. purpurea has hairs distributed over the calyx-tube surface. D. enneandra exposes much more rachis in a loose spike; D. tenuis is consistently 3-foliolate with extremely narrow leaflets and smaller globose heads. Do not identify D. purpurea primarily by purple flower color.

required_roles: flower-head progression from lower to upper flowers
side-by-side D. purpurea versus D. compacta calyx comparison
